claims.text: The initial CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a well-equilibrated, homogeneous microstructure with minimal pre-existing carbides.
Carburizing CoCrFeMnNi in a methane/hydrogen atmosphere at 950°C introduces interstitial carbon.
An optimal carbon content produces finely dispersed carbide precipitates along grain boundaries and within grains.
Fine carbide precipitates strengthen grain boundaries.
Fine carbide precipitates retard crack initiation.
Grain-boundary strengthening and delayed crack initiation improve toughness.
Coarse carbide precipitates create brittle regions.
Brittle regions associated with coarse carbides reduce toughness.
Approximately one hour of carburization at 950°C will increase fracture toughness relative to untreated CoCrFeMnNi.
Approximately one hour of carburization at 950°C will increase impact resistance relative to untreated CoCrFeMnNi.
Two hours of carburization at 950°C will cause measurable toughness deterioration relative to the optimal treatment.
The predicted toughness deterioration after two hours is caused by coarse carbide formation.
The proposed behavior is expected to hold at 950°C for treatment durations from 0.5 to 2 hours under the specified atmosphere and quenching conditions.
Changes in temperature, carburizing atmosphere, or quenching rate may produce different microstructural evolution.
Microstructural heterogeneity can alter the balance between beneficial fine carbides and detrimental coarse carbides.
The magnitude of toughness improvement or degradation can vary with processing variations.
In-situ TEM can precisely track and control carbide nucleation and growth during the specified carburization treatment.
